sections.section_title: Dermatomyositis in Context: Core Disease Concepts and the Significance of Pseudoangioedema
sections.description: This section introduces the background medical knowledge needed to understand the case, focusing on dermatomyositis as an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy, its usual organ involvement, and why oedematous neck swelling is a misleading but important atypical presentation. It also frames the relevance of anti-SAE1 antibodies and the concept of pseudoangioedema in inflammatory myopathy.
subtopics: Definition and epidemiology of dermatomyositis
Typical clinical domains: skin, skeletal muscle, swallowing, lungs, heart, and gastrointestinal involvement
Immunopathology of dermatomyositis: microangiopathy, perifascicular injury, and complement-mediated capillary damage
Classic cutaneous findings: Gottron’s papules, heliotrope rash, shawl sign, V-neck sign, holster sign, and periungual changes
Mechanisms of dysphagia and respiratory compromise in inflammatory myopathy
Subcutaneous oedema and pseudoangioedema in dermatomyositis: rarity, proposed mechanisms, and why it mimics angioedema
Overview of myositis-specific autoantibodies with emphasis on anti-SAE1 phenotype
Clinical associations of SAE1-positive dermatomyositis: prominent skin disease, dysphagia, interstitial lung disease risk, and malignancy association

sections.section_title: Initial Presentation and Diagnostic Reframing: From Neck Swelling to Suspected Inflammatory Myopathy
sections.description: This section follows the patient’s early clinical course and shows how the working diagnosis shifted from deep neck infection and angioedema toward dermatomyositis. It emphasizes the bedside clues, pattern recognition, and red flags that prompted clinicians to reconsider the initial assumptions.
subtopics: Clinical summary of the presenting illness: progressive neck swelling, proximal weakness, and mild myalgia
Why Ludwig’s angina and deep neck space infection were initially suspected
Interpretation of early CT neck findings showing diffuse oedema and retropharyngeal inflammation
ENT assessment and the significance of a normal structural examination with increased secretions and coughing
Features arguing against infectious neck pathology: afebrile state, airway stability, and lack of focal suppuration
Why the presentation was atypical for histaminergic or bradykinin-mediated angioedema
Medication and family history review in the assessment of unexplained angioedema
Importance of subtle examination findings: periungual erythema, nailfold microhaemorrhages, avascular areas, facial erythema, and thigh rash
Clinical significance of proximal hip flexor weakness in the setting of neck swelling
The pivotal role of ordering creatine kinase in unexplained soft tissue swelling with muscle or skin clues

sections.section_title: Definitive Workup and Diagnostic Reasoning: Establishing SAE1-Positive Dermatomyositis
sections.description: This section explains how laboratory testing, imaging, functional studies, serology, and tissue pathology were integrated to confirm the diagnosis. It also teaches learners how to reason through competing diagnoses and interpret findings that distinguish dermatomyositis from other causes of neck swelling and weakness.
subtopics: Interpretation of markedly elevated creatine kinase, transaminases, and lactate dehydrogenase in myositis
Why normal renal function and negative urine myoglobin did not exclude significant muscle inflammation
Angioedema laboratory evaluation: C3, C4, C1 esterase level, and function
Autoimmune serology: ANA pattern and the diagnostic value of myositis-specific antibodies
Anti-SAE1 antibody testing: what it means and how it supports phenotype recognition
MRI of the thighs in inflammatory myopathy: detecting active muscle inflammation and selecting biopsy targets
FDG-PET findings in diffuse myositis and its role in excluding occult malignancy
Assessment of swallowing dysfunction with video fluoroscopic swallow study
Pulmonary assessment: restrictive physiology, aspiration-related changes, and evaluation for interstitial lung disease
Muscle biopsy hallmarks of dermatomyositis: perifascicular necrosis/regeneration, perimysial inflammation, and C5b-9 capillary deposition
Diagnostic synthesis: why this case met clinicopathologic criteria for dermatomyositis

Focused differential diagnosis: immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, inclusion body myositis, myasthenia gravis, cellulitis/erysipelas, deep neck infection, sialadenitis, drug hypersensitivity, urticarial vasculitis, superior vena cava syndrome, and contact or granulomatous disorders

sections.section_title: Management Strategy in Severe Dermatomyositis with Airway and Swallowing Involvement
sections.description: This section details the treatment decisions made in response to severe disease manifestations, especially cervical swelling, dysphagia, and widespread active myositis. It highlights the rationale for combination immunosuppression, medication selection, supportive care, and risk mitigation during treatment.
subtopics: Principles of urgent treatment in moderate to severe dermatomyositis
Indications for pulse intravenous methylprednisolone in threatened airway or major bulbar involvement
Transition to high-dose oral prednisone and tapering strategy
Role of intravenous immunoglobulin in severe myositis and dysphagia
Mycophenolate mofetil as a steroid-sparing agent: rationale, benefits, and monitoring
Use of rituximab in refractory or high-risk inflammatory myopathy phenotypes
Why methotrexate was avoided in this patient with abnormal lung assessment and concern for pulmonary toxicity
Alternative steroid-sparing options such as azathioprine and tacrolimus, and why they were not chosen here
Supportive management of severe dysphagia: aspiration risk reduction, nutrition, and nasogastric feeding
Recognition and treatment of aspiration pneumonitis in the context of pharyngeal weakness
Infection prevention during intensive immunosuppression, including Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis
Adverse effect management: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole-associated haemolytic anaemia and switch to nebulised pentamidine
Baseline infectious screening before immunosuppression: hepatitis, HIV, tuberculosis, VZV, and CMV

sections.section_title: Outcome, Surveillance, and Clinical Lessons for Practice
sections.description: This final section reviews the patient’s recovery, longitudinal monitoring, malignancy screening implications, and the broader teaching points for clinicians. It translates the case into practical lessons about recognizing atypical dermatomyositis and avoiding diagnostic delay when neck swelling is not true angioedema.
subtopics: Short-term inpatient response: improvement in neck swelling and hip flexor weakness
Time course of laboratory recovery, including creatine kinase normalization
Persistent dysphagia and delayed functional recovery despite early biochemical improvement
Resolution of cutaneous and cervical findings over follow-up
Longer-term outcomes: steroid discontinuation, stable strength, and respiratory recovery
Follow-up imaging and pulmonary function trends after aspiration-related lung changes
Malignancy risk stratification in dermatomyositis using IMACS principles
Why this patient qualified as high risk for cancer: dermatomyositis, dysphagia, male sex, and SAE1 positivity
Components of malignancy screening in myositis: CT imaging, PET, tumour markers, symptom review, examination, and planned endoscopy
Monitoring for relapse, medication toxicity, and need for adjustment of long-term immunosuppression
Key diagnostic pearl: unexplained localized neck swelling with nailfold or rash findings should prompt consideration of dermatomyositis
Key systems-based lesson: collaboration among emergency medicine, ENT, immunology, rheumatology, radiology, pathology, and speech/swallow services
How this case refines the differential diagnosis of angioedema and pseudoangioedema in acute care settings
